cards.front: In vertebrate blood, why is partial pressure of oxygen (PO2) not the same thing as the amount of oxygen?
cards.back: Most of the blood's oxygen is bound to haemoglobin, which adds to the amount without raising the PO2. PO2 is the pressure oxygen would exert alone.
cards.quote: most of its oxygen is bound to haemoglobin, which adds to the amount without raising the PO2

cards.front: Gas crosses exchange surfaces only by diffusion. What ceiling does that set on the PO2 of blood that takes up oxygen all along a surface?
cards.back: It can leave with no higher PO2 than the water or air it last touched, because diffusion only pulls the blood's partial pressure toward that of the medium beside it.
cards.quote: So blood that takes up oxygen all along the surface can leave with no higher PO2 than the water or air it last touched

cards.front: Name conditions that leave real blood below the partial-pressure ceiling of an exchange surface.
cards.back: A small or thick surface, short contact time, mismatched air (or water) and blood flow, or blood that bypasses the surface.
cards.quote: A small or thick surface, short contact time, mismatched air and blood flow, or blood that bypasses the surface leave real blood below it.

cards.front: Fick's law for a sheet of tissue: rate of gas transfer = {{c1::k x A x (P1 - P2) / T}}
cards.back: A = area, P1 - P2 = partial-pressure difference, T = barrier thickness, k = a constant for that gas and barrier.
cards.quote: rate of gas transfer = k x A x (P1 - P2) / T
cards.section: Fick's law: how fast gas crosses

cards.front: Dry air at sea level is about 21% oxygen at about 760 mmHg, giving a PO2 of roughly 160 mmHg. A hypothetical gas mixture is also 21% oxygen but at a total pressure of 380 mmHg. What is its PO2?
cards.back: Partial pressure = fraction x total pressure: 0.21 x 380 mmHg = about 80 mmHg, half the sea-level value.
cards.quote: dry air at sea level (about 21% oxygen at about 760 mmHg, 101 kPa) has a PO2 of roughly 160 mmHg (21 kPa)
cards.section: Fick's law: how fast gas crosses

cards.front: Surface A is 80 m2 with a 0.6 micrometre barrier; surface B is 60 m2 with a 0.3 micrometre barrier. Same gas, partial-pressure difference and material. What is B's rate relative to A's?
cards.back: Rate B / Rate A = (A_B / A_A) x (T_A / T_B) = (60/80) x (0.6/0.3) = 0.75 x 2 = 1.5. B transfers 1.5 times as fast.
cards.why: k and the partial-pressure difference cancel; thickness flips because it sits below the line in Fick's law.
cards.quote: Rate 2 / Rate 1 = (A2 / A1) x (T1 / T2), since k and ΔP cancel
cards.section: Fick's law: how fast gas crosses

cards.front: Air-saturated fresh water at 15 to 20 degrees C holds roughly {{c1::30 times}} less oxygen per litre than air.
cards.quote: air-saturated fresh water at 15 to 20 degrees C holds roughly 30 times less oxygen per litre than air
cards.section: Water or air: skin, gills and tracheae

cards.front: Why is breathing water harder than breathing air?
cards.back: Water holds far less oxygen per litre and is about 800 times denser and far more viscous, so a gill does more work for less oxygen.
cards.quote: it is about 800 times denser and far more viscous, so a gill does more work for less oxygen
cards.section: Water or air: skin, gills and tracheae

cards.front: Under what conditions does breathing through the skin work, as in earthworms and lungless salamanders?
cards.back: Where the skin stays wet and oxygen demand per unit of surface is modest.
cards.quote: Skin breathing works where skin stays wet and oxygen demand per unit of surface is modest.
cards.section: Water or air: skin, gills and tracheae

cards.front: In a teleost gill lamella, how do blood and water flow relative to each other, and what PO2 ceiling does that set for the leaving blood?
cards.back: In opposite directions (countercurrent). Leaving blood last touches incoming water, so its ceiling is the PO2 of the incoming water.
cards.quote: Blood runs opposite to the water inside each lamella
cards.section: Water or air: skin, gills and tracheae

cards.front: A trout with plenty of lamellar area pumps only a trickle of water past its gills, carrying less oxygen per minute than its blood could take up. Does countercurrent flow still bring the leaving blood close to the incoming water's PO2?
cards.back: No. The ceiling is unchanged, but the trickle loses much of its oxygen on the way, so its PO2 falls toward the blood's before the blood is full.
cards.why: Getting near the ceiling takes a large, thin surface and a water flow whose oxygen-carrying capacity per minute is at least the blood's.
cards.quote: Getting near the incoming water takes both a large, thin surface and a water flow whose oxygen-carrying capacity per minute is at least the blood's.
cards.section: Water or air: skin, gills and tracheae

cards.front: Apply the diffusion ceiling to carbon dioxide in a teleost gill with countercurrent flow. What is the lowest PCO2 the blood leaving the gill can reach?
cards.back: The PCO2 of the incoming water, the water it last touched. Blood that gives up carbon dioxide all along can leave with no lower PCO2 than that.
cards.quote: and blood that gives up carbon dioxide all along, with no lower PCO2

cards.front: Most insects carry oxygen in air, not blood: air enters openings called spiracles into {{c1::tracheae}}, branching tubes whose finest branches reach the tissues.
cards.quote: Most insects carry oxygen in air, not blood: air enters openings called spiracles into tracheae, branching tubes whose finest branches reach the tissues.
cards.section: Water or air: skin, gills and tracheae

cards.front: Synchrotron X-ray imaging of live beetles, crickets and ants (Westneat and colleagues, 2003) showed what about insect tracheae?
cards.back: The tracheae compress and expand rhythmically in live beetles, crickets and ants; many larger insects also pump the abdomen.
cards.quote: used synchrotron X-ray imaging to watch tracheae in live beetles, crickets and ants compress and expand rhythmically
cards.section: Water or air: skin, gills and tracheae

cards.front: A trout's gill can send blood out at a higher PO2 than the water leaving the gill. Why can a mammal lung not send blood out above the PO2 of the air it exhales?
cards.back: Gill blood last touches incoming water (countercurrent). Mammal alveolar blood last touches mixed alveolar gas in dead-ended sacs, so it can at best match that gas, not fresher air.
cards.why: Rests on the diffusion ceiling: blood can at best match the medium it last touched, and the flow arrangement sets what that is.
cards.quote: yet a trout's gill can send its blood out at a higher oxygen partial pressure than the water leaving it

cards.front: In a resting adult human, alveolar PO2 sits near {{c1::100 mmHg}}, below the roughly 150 mmHg of warmed, humidified inhaled air.
cards.quote: Their PO2 sits near 100 mmHg in a resting adult human, below the roughly 150 mmHg of warmed, humidified inhaled air
cards.section: Three lungs: mammal, bird, alligator

cards.front: What is tidal ventilation, as in mammal lungs?
cards.back: Air flows in and out through the same airways, into dead-ended sacs, the alveoli.
cards.quote: Air flows in and out through the same airways, tidal ventilation, into tiny dead-ended sacs, the alveoli.
cards.section: Three lungs: mammal, bird, alligator

cards.front: In a bird's parabronchi, capillaries cross the parabronchus at right angles, each at a different point along it: {{c1::crosscurrent}} exchange.
cards.back: Air sacs act as bellows; air flows one way through most parabronchi during both inspiration and expiration.
cards.quote: Capillaries cross the parabronchus at right angles, each at a different point along it: crosscurrent exchange.
cards.section: Three lungs: mammal, bird, alligator

cards.front: In a bird lung, how can mixed blood leaving the parabronchi carry a higher PO2 than the air leaving them?
cards.back: Capillaries near the inflow end match nearly fresh air; those near the outflow end match drained air. Mixing their oxygen contents lands the blood between richest and poorest streams, above the outflow air.
cards.quote: so the mixed blood lands between its richest and poorest streams and can carry a higher PO2 than the air leaving the parabronchi
cards.section: Three lungs: mammal, bird, alligator

cards.front: Idealized countercurrent (gill), crosscurrent (bird lung) and tidal (mammal lung) arrangements get the same incoming PO2, matched medium-to-blood capacity ratios, even flow and no diffusion limit. Rank the leaving-blood PO2 and explain.
cards.back: Gill > bird lung > mammal lung. Gill blood last touches incoming water; bird blood a spread of air from fresh to drained; mammal blood mixed alveolar gas.
cards.why: Ranks idealized shapes, not real animals.
cards.quote: The gill's leaving blood last touches incoming water; the bird's, a spread of air from fresh to drained; the mammal's, mixed alveolar gas.
cards.section: Three lungs: mammal, bird, alligator

cards.front: One-way airflow occurs in birds and in American alligators (both archosaurs) and also in monitor lizards and green iguanas. What histories does this distribution allow?
cards.back: The trait may be older than archosaurs, or may have evolved more than once. Sharing between birds and crocodilians fits common ancestry without proving it.
cards.quote: so the trait may be older than archosaurs, or may have evolved more than once
cards.section: Three lungs: mammal, bird, alligator

cards.front: In quiet human inspiration, the {{c1::external intercostal}} muscles lift the ribs as the diaphragm contracts, and the lungs follow the enlarging chest.
cards.quote: The external intercostal muscles lift the ribs as the diaphragm contracts, and the lungs follow the enlarging chest.
cards.section: Moving the gas: aspiration and the frog's pump

cards.front: In adult humans, what drives quiet expiration, and what is added for forceful expiration?
cards.back: Quiet: passive recoil of lungs and chest wall once the muscles relax. Forceful: internal intercostals and abdominal muscles.
cards.quote: Quiet expiration in adult humans is normally passive recoil of lungs and chest wall once the muscles relax
cards.section: Moving the gas: aspiration and the frog's pump

cards.front: What does pulmonary surfactant do, and why does it make breathing easier?
cards.back: It lowers the surface tension of the wet alveolar lining, raising compliance (stretch per pressure change), so the lung inflates with less effort.
cards.quote: Surfactant, a lipid and protein mixture secreted by alveolar cells, lowers it, raising compliance
cards.section: Moving the gas: aspiration and the frog's pump

cards.front: A lung's alveolar cells secrete too little surfactant. Predict the effect on surface tension, compliance and the effort of inflation.
cards.back: Surface tension would be higher than with normal surfactant, pulling the alveoli inward; compliance falls, so inflation takes more effort.
cards.why: Surfactant normally lowers surface tension and raises compliance; removing it reverses both.
cards.quote: The wet lining of the alveoli has surface tension, pulling inward like a soap bubble.
cards.section: Moving the gas: aspiration and the frog's pump

cards.front: How does a frog fill its lungs by buccal pumping, and how does that differ from mammal and bird breathing?
cards.back: Mouth floor drops with nostrils open (air in); nostrils close, glottis opens, floor rises, pushing air in under positive pressure. Mammals and birds instead draw air in by lowering pressure.
cards.quote: then closes the nostrils, opens the glottis (the opening into the airway) and raises the floor, pushing air into the lungs under positive pressure
cards.section: Moving the gas: aspiration and the frog's pump

cards.front: Haldane and Priestley needed alveolar gas from resting subjects. Why did they sample the end of a forced breath out rather than windpipe gas?
cards.back: Windpipe gas mixes fresh and stale air; the end of a forced expiration approximates alveolar air.
cards.quote: because windpipe gas mixes fresh and stale air, they took the end of a forced breath out as alveolar air
cards.section: Carbon dioxide runs the controller

cards.front: Name the two kinds of chemoreceptor that drive breathing in mammals and what each mainly senses.
cards.back: Central chemoreceptors: pH of brain extracellular fluid. Carotid bodies (at the carotid fork): mainly low arterial oxygen, also affected by carbon dioxide.
cards.quote: the carotid bodies, sensory clusters where each carotid artery forks, which respond mainly to low arterial oxygen and are also affected by carbon dioxide
cards.section: Carbon dioxide runs the controller

cards.front: In adult humans, when does low oxygen (hypoxia) raise ventilation steeply?
cards.back: Only once arterial PO2 falls well below normal. In adult humans at rest, carbon dioxide is the main stimulus (Haldane and Priestley's result in resting subjects).
cards.quote: In adult humans, ventilation rises steeply with hypoxia, too little oxygen, only once arterial PO2 falls well below normal.
cards.section: Carbon dioxide runs the controller

cards.front: The water around a resting teleost fish loses much of its oxygen. Predict the change in the fish's gill ventilation.
cards.back: Ventilation rises, because in teleosts low oxygen in the water is a major ventilatory stimulus.
cards.quote: In teleosts, low oxygen in the water is a major ventilatory stimulus.
cards.section: Carbon dioxide runs the controller

cards.front: A resting person breathes a low-oxygen gas mixture that drops arterial PO2 well below normal; ventilation rises steeply while carbon dioxide production stays the same. Which sensor mainly drives the rise, and what happens to alveolar PCO2?
cards.back: Mainly the carotid bodies, responding to low arterial oxygen. Breathing now exceeds what production requires, so alveolar PCO2 falls (hypocapnia).
cards.quote: Mainly the carotid bodies, which respond to low arterial oxygen; nothing here raised carbon dioxide.
cards.section: Carbon dioxide runs the controller

cards.front: Dead space is the {{c1::conducting airways}}, which have no alveoli and exchange no gas; about 150 mL in an illustrative resting adult.
cards.quote: 150 mL of dead space, the conducting airways, which have no alveoli and exchange no gas
cards.section: Carbon dioxide runs the controller

cards.front: How do minute ventilation and alveolar ventilation differ, and how is each calculated?
cards.back: Minute ventilation = total air moved = rate x tidal volume. Alveolar ventilation = fresh air reaching alveoli = rate x (tidal volume - dead space).
cards.quote: Alveolar ventilation, fresh air reaching alveoli, = 12 x (500 - 150) = 4,200 mL per minute.
cards.section: Carbon dioxide runs the controller

cards.front: Dead space is 150 mL. Breathing pattern A: 10 breaths per minute of 600 mL. Pattern B: 20 breaths per minute of 300 mL. Compare minute and alveolar ventilation.
cards.why: Each breath wastes the same dead space, so shallower, faster breathing delivers less fresh air.
cards.quote: Breathe rapidly and shallowly, 24 breaths of 250 mL: minute ventilation = 24 x 250 = 6,000 mL per minute, unchanged.
cards.section: Carbon dioxide runs the controller

cards.front: At steady state on ordinary air, alveolar PCO2 is about 0.863 x CO2 production (mL/min) / alveolar ventilation (L/min). With production at 200 mL/min and alveolar ventilation of 3.0 L/min, what is alveolar PCO2?
cards.quote: At steady state, breathing ordinary air, alveolar PCO2 is about 0.863 x carbon dioxide production (mL per minute) / alveolar ventilation (L per minute).
cards.section: Carbon dioxide runs the controller

cards.front: Carbon dioxide production stays constant while alveolar ventilation doubles. What happens to alveolar PCO2 at the new steady state?
cards.back: It falls to about half, because alveolar PCO2 is proportional to production divided by alveolar ventilation.
cards.quote: With production held at an illustrative 200 mL per minute, alveolar PCO2 would rise from about 41 to about 72 mmHg.
cards.section: Carbon dioxide runs the controller

cards.front: A resting person switches to rapid, shallow breathing with unchanged minute ventilation and unchanged carbon dioxide production. Predict alveolar PCO2 and the effect on the drive to breathe.
cards.back: Alveolar ventilation falls (more of each breath is dead space), so alveolar PCO2 rises. Since carbon dioxide is the main resting stimulus, the drive to breathe increases.
cards.why: Combines the dead-space calculation, PCO2 proportional to production over alveolar ventilation, and carbon dioxide as the main resting drive.
cards.quote: Alveolar ventilation = 24 x (250 - 150) = 2,400 mL per minute, 57% of before.
cards.section: Carbon dioxide runs the controller

cards.front: Directional flow probes show one-way flow in a bronchus of an excised alligator lung pumped in and out through the trachea. What control rules out faulty probes or pump, and what does persistence of one-way flow show?
cards.back: Control: a mammal lung on the same pump should show flow reversing with each breath. If one-way flow persists without flap valves, the lung's own structure, most likely airway geometry, produces it.
cards.quote: As a control, a mammal lung on the same pump should show flow reversing with each breath; if not, the probes or pump are at fault.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Idealized models rank countercurrent above crosscurrent above a mammal's mixed pool. Why do the arrangements barely differ when the exchange surface is small or thick?
cards.back: When the surface is small or thick, the arrangements barely differ (per the lesson): blood stays well below any ceiling, so the higher ceiling a flow arrangement sets is rarely approached.
cards.why: Rests on Fick's law and the rule that a small or thick surface leaves real blood below the ceiling.
cards.quote: When the surface is small or thick, the arrangements barely differ.
cards.section: Ranking flow arrangements, and a tracer aside

cards.front: Disease triples the thickness of an alveolar barrier while area and partial-pressure difference stay the same. Predict the diffusion rate and whether the PO2 ceiling for leaving blood changes.
cards.back: The rate falls to one third. The ceiling (alveolar gas PO2) is unchanged, but the blood is now more likely to leave below it.
cards.why: Fick's law puts thickness below the line; a thick surface leaves real blood below the ceiling.
cards.quote: thickness flips because it sits below the line
cards.section: Fick's law: how fast gas crosses

cards.front: Is it strictly true that air takes two breaths to pass through a bird lung?
cards.back: No, that is a schematic. Helium tracer work in songbirds found some inhaled gas reaching the front air sacs within one breath.
cards.quote: helium tracer work in songbirds found some inhaled gas reaching the front air sacs within one breath
cards.section: Ranking flow arrangements, and a tracer aside

cards.front: In mice, which two pH sensors do retrotrapezoid nucleus neurons use to sense carbon dioxide?
cards.back: The proton-sensing receptor GPR4 and the potassium channel TASK-2, working in parallel; losing GPR4 alone removes much of the response.
cards.quote: retrotrapezoid nucleus neurons carry two pH sensors that work in parallel, the proton-sensing receptor GPR4 and the potassium channel TASK-2
cards.section: Sensing carbon dioxide in the brainstem
